summary: Describes how the restrictions on the IPv6 flow label apply when it is used for load balancing by equal cost multipath routing and link aggregation. It focuses on IP-in-IPv6 tunnels, where the outer header can carry a label for spreading traffic across paths.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6438 explains how to spread tunneled traffic evenly over several equal cost network paths. The tunnel endpoint writes a value into the 20-bit flow label of the outer IPv6 header, and the routers in between use that value when they hash a packet to choose an outgoing link. This works even though the routers cannot see the packets inside the tunnel.

subtitle: How tunnel endpoints and routers can use the IPv6 flow label to spread traffic over equal cost paths.

tldr.problem: When many equal cost paths exist between two routers, traffic must be spread across them. In an IP-in-IPv6 tunnel every packet has the same outer source and destination addresses, so the usual hash of the address pair is constant and all the traffic lands on one path.
tldr.mechanism: The tunnel endpoint sets a 20-bit flow label in the outer IPv6 header, chosen from a uniform distribution and the same for every packet of one user flow. Routers then include {dest addr, source addr, flow label} in the hash that picks the outgoing link.
tldr.outcome: Tunneled traffic can be load-balanced without looking inside the tunnel, which matters most for IPv6 where the transport ports are hard to extract. The document is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6438 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2011 and has not been obsoleted. It applies to both RFC 3697 and its revision RFC 6437, which the RFC states is fully compatible with it and removes the concerns raised by the older flow label rules.

sections.title: Equal Cost Multipath and Link Aggregation
sections.content:
When the routing system knows that several paths between the same two nodes are equally good in capacity and latency, it can be useful to share traffic among them. Two techniques do this: equal cost multipath (ECMP) routing and link aggregation (LAG). Several goals have to be met at once. The traffic share on each path should stay roughly equal, or appropriately weighted when the paths differ in capacity. Out-of-order delivery within an individual flow should be avoided as far as possible. Idle time on any path should be minimised when a queue elsewhere is not empty.

These goals can conflict. Strictly avoiding idle time could let a small packet sent on an idle path overtake a larger packet from the same flow, which is out-of-order delivery.

The lightweight approach described here is a modulo(N) hash over a defined set of packet header fields, where N is the number of equally good paths. The fields chosen are certain to hold the same values for the whole duration of a flow, and the hash output selects a path. If the hash function has a uniform statistical distribution, the traffic is shared roughly equally. Because the hash input is consistent across a flow, all packets of that flow produce the same output, so no reordering happens within the flow. With a large number of distinct flows, each link's queue also stays non-empty, which avoids idle paths.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router has several equally good ways to reach the same destination, it can split traffic across them. A common way is to hash certain header fields of each packet and pick the path by the result. Packets of the same flow hash the same way, so they all take the same path and stay in order.

sections.title: Choosing Header Fields for the Hash
sections.content:
Throughout the document a flow is a sequence of packets identified either by the source and destination IP addresses alone, the 2-tuple, or by source address, destination address, protocol number, source port and destination port, the 5-tuple. The 5-tuple is more specifically called a microflow in RFC 2474, but that term is not used in connection with the flow label in RFC 3697.

For general traffic a common choice is a hash of the 2-tuple. That is necessary and sufficient to avoid out-of-order delivery, and with the variety of sources and destinations found in the core of the network it is often statistically enough to distribute the load evenly. In practice many implementations use the 5-tuple, because the protocol number and port numbers add 40 bits and improve the distribution thanks to the variability of ephemeral ports, which are well distributed and typically contribute 16 variable bits. Including transport-layer information can be a problem for IP fragments and for encrypted traffic.

In IPv6 the 5-tuple is inconvenient to extract, because the next-header fields vary in placement and length, so every implementation must be able to skip over next-headers even when they rarely appear. RFC 2460 implies that next-headers other than hop-by-hop options are not normally inspected by intermediate nodes, so some hardware implementations may struggle, and network equipment vendors might cut the number of fields they take from an IPv6 header. A Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) header and a GRE key create a similar difficulty, and anything that complicates header analysis is undesirable.

The situation is different in IP-in-IP tunneled scenarios. Identifying a flow inside a tunnel is more complicated, because nearly all hardware can only identify flows from the outermost IP header. Suppose traffic from many sources to many destinations is aggregated in a single IP-in-IP tunnel from tunnel endpoint A to tunnel endpoint B. All packets forming the tunnel have outer source address A and outer destination address B, and in all probability the same port and protocol numbers. If ECMP or LAG is applied between routers R1 and R2, the 2-tuple or 5-tuple and its hash are constant, so no load sharing is achieved: polarization occurs. If a high proportion of traffic comes from one or a small number of tunnels, the traffic is not distributed as intended across the paths between R1 and R2, which is partial polarization.
sections.plainLanguage: The hash needs fields that do not change during a flow. Source and destination addresses work, and adding the protocol and ports spreads traffic better. But in IPv6 those transport fields sit behind variable-length extension headers, so routers often cannot read them cheaply. Inside a tunnel, the outer addresses are the same for every packet, so hashing them sends all the traffic down one path.

sections.title: The Flow Label Rules
sections.content:
The flow label was left Experimental by RFC 2460 and was better defined by RFC 3697. Three rules from that document are quoted. The flow label value set by the source must be delivered unchanged to the destination nodes. IPv6 nodes must not assume any mathematical or other properties of the flow label values assigned by source nodes. Router performance should not depend on the distribution of the flow label values, and especially the flow label bits alone make poor material for a hash key.

These rules, and the last one in particular, made designers hesitant to use the flow label for ECMP or LAG. Most nodes set a zero value in the flow label, and the first rule forbids the routing system from changing the flow label once a packet has left the source node. For normal IPv6 traffic a typically zero flow label would add nothing to an ECMP or LAG hash, though it would do no harm to the distribution of the hash values either.

In an IP-in-IPv6 tunnel, however, the tunnel endpoint is itself the source node of the outer packets, so it may freely set a flow label in the outer IPv6 header of the packets it sends into the tunnel. The second and third rules have to be read in the context of RFC 3697, which assumes that routers using the flow label take part in some method of establishing flow state, so that flow state is established on all or a subset of the IPv6 nodes on the path. A router that knows the properties of the resulting flow label values can rely on them without further signalling, and rule 2 does not apply to it; it can also deviate from rule 3. In the tunnel situation, routers R1 and R2 can rely on the flow labels set by the tunnel endpoints being assigned by a known method. An ECMP or LAG method can therefore be based on the flow label consistently with RFC 3697, whether or not the non-tunnel traffic carries non-zero flow label values.

The IETF has since revised RFC 3697 in RFC 6437. That revision is fully compatible with this document and removes the concerns that came from the three rules above, so this specification applies both to RFC 3697 and to RFC 6437.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier IPv6 rules told routers not to depend on the flow label, because most senders left it at zero and the label was not protected. A tunnel endpoint is different: it creates the outer header, so it chooses the label itself, and the routers on the path can be told how it is chosen. The newer flow label specification, RFC 6437, settles this.

sections.title: Guidelines
sections.content:
The guidelines assume that the routers supporting ECMP or LAG, R1 and R2 in the figure, do not know they are handling tunneled traffic. If the IPv6 flow label is to be included in an ECMP or LAG hash in that scenario, the following apply.

Inner packets must be encapsulated in an outer IPv6 packet whose source and destination addresses are those of the tunnel endpoints. The flow label in the outer packet should be set by the sending tunnel endpoint to a 20-bit value in accordance with RFC 6437, and the same flow label value must be used for all packets in a single user flow, as determined by the IP header fields of the inner packet. To achieve this, the sending endpoint must classify all packets into flows once it has decided they should enter a given tunnel, and then write the relevant flow label into the outer IPv6 header. A user flow can be identified by the sending endpoint most simply by its {destination, source} address 2-tuple or by its 5-tuple; using the {dest addr, source addr, flow label} 3-tuple of the inner packet would be a future-proof option, and the choice of n-tuple is an implementation choice in the sending endpoint.

As specified in RFC 6437, the flow label values should be chosen from a uniform distribution. Such values suit a load-balancing hash function and are hard for a malicious third party to predict. The sending endpoint may perform stateless flow label assignment by using a suitable 20-bit hash of the inner IP header's 2-tuple or 5-tuple as the label value. If the inner packet is an IPv6 packet, its flow label value could also be included in this hash. This stateless method creates a small probability that two different user flows hash to the same label; since RFC 6437 allows a source to define any set of packets as a single flow, occasionally labelling two user flows as one flow through the tunnel is acceptable.

At intermediate routers that perform load distribution, the hash algorithm used to determine the outgoing component link must minimally include the 3-tuple {dest addr, source addr, flow label}, and may also include the remaining components of the 5-tuple. This applies whether the traffic is tunneled only or a mixture of tunneled and normal traffic. Because an intermediate IPv6 router will probably meet a mixture of tunneled and normal traffic, the design should also include {protocol, dest port, source port} as input keys, to give additional entropy for flows whose flow label is zero, including non-tunneled traffic flows.

Individual nodes are free to implement different algorithms that conform to this specification without affecting the interoperability or function of the network. Operations, administration and maintenance techniques will need to be adapted to manage ECMP and LAG based on the flow label, with issues similar to those that arise for MPLS and pseudowires.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel endpoint reads the inner packet headers, works out which flow the packet belongs to, and writes a label for that flow into the outer IPv6 header. Every packet of the same flow gets the same label. The routers in between then hash the outer address pair and the label, and add the protocol and ports when they can, so that flows with a zero label still spread out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The flow label is not protected in any way and can be forged by an on-path attacker. It is expected, however, that tunnel endpoints and the ECMP or LAG paths will be part of a managed infrastructure that is well protected against on-path attacks, for example by using IPsec between the two tunnel endpoints. Off-path attackers are unlikely to guess a valid flow label if an apparently pseudo-random and unpredictable value is used. In either case, the worst an attacker could do against ECMP or LAG is try to selectively overload a particular path. The RFC refers the reader to RFC 6437 for further discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing protects the flow label, so an attacker on the path could change it. The expected answer is that tunnels run inside a managed and protected network. Even then, the most an attacker could achieve is to push traffic onto one path and overload it.

viz.caption: Candidate hash inputs for equal cost multipath

cells: Source and destination addresses. Necessary and sufficient to avoid out-of-order delivery, and often statistically sufficient in the network core.
Adds protocol and port numbers, 40 bits in total. Improves the hash distribution but is inconvenient to extract in IPv6 and is a problem for fragments and encrypted traffic.
The 20-bit IPv6 flow label replaces the port numbers and protocol number as hash input where the inner header is inaccessible, as in a tunnel.

items.title: Delivered unchanged
items.text: The flow label value set by the source must reach the destination nodes unchanged.

items.title: No assumed properties
items.text: IPv6 nodes must not assume any mathematical or other properties of the flow label values.

items.title: Poor hash material
items.text: Router performance should not depend on the distribution of the values, and the label bits alone make a poor hash key.
